summary:
**Planet X and SPHEREx: Multi-Epoch Infrared Transient Detection Pipeline**

We developed an automated pipeline for astronomical data retrieval and image analysis using NASA's SPHEREx Data Release 1 (DR1) archive via the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). Built primarily with **Python**, the system uses **Astroquery** to retrieve infrared FITS observations through the Simple Image Access (SIA2) service. We use **Astropy** for FITS processing and World Coordinate System (WCS) handling, **NumPy** for numerical operations, and **Reproject** for precise sky-image alignment. The pipeline also applies NaN-value handling, median imputation, and ZScale intensity normalization before generating difference maps between observations from two epochs separated by approximately 407 days.

Our project addresses the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge by demonstrating how multi-epoch infrared observations can help investigate potential moving objects and transient sources, including asteroids. By automating data retrieval, preprocessing, WCS reprojection, and image differencing, it provides a foundation for efficient astronomical exploration.

This work matters because systematically comparing repeated sky observations can reveal changes that might otherwise go unnoticed, helping researchers identify and prioritize interesting celestial candidates for further study, including objects in our Solar System.
details:
Project Details: Planet X and SPHEREx — Multi-Epoch Infrared Transient Detection Pipeline

Our project is an automated astronomical data retrieval, preprocessing, WCS sky-alignment, and multi-epoch image-differencing pipeline developed using NASA's SPHEREx Data Release 1 (DR1) archive through the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA).

How It Works

The pipeline retrieves infrared astronomical observations of the same sky region from two different epochs using NASA's Simple Image Access (SIA2) service. For our demonstration, we compare observations from April 29, 2025, and June 10, 2026, in the SPHEREx-D1 spectral band, providing an approximately 407-day observation baseline.

The retrieved FITS images undergo preprocessing, including NaN-value handling, median imputation, and ZScale intensity normalization. We extract World Coordinate System (WCS) information and use image reprojection to align the second observation with the first on a common pixel grid. Finally, we subtract the aligned images to generate difference maps that highlight potential changes, transient sources, and moving-object candidates against the relatively stationary background.

Technologies and Tools

Our project uses Python and the following technologies:

  • Astroquery: Automated retrieval of astronomical observations from NASA IRSA.
  • Astropy: FITS file handling, astronomical coordinates, and WCS processing.
  • NumPy: Numerical operations and image-array processing.
  • Reproject: WCS-based image alignment and reprojection.
  • Matplotlib: Astronomical image visualization and difference-map plotting.
  • FITS: Standard astronomical image data format.
  • NASA IRSA and SIA2: Access to authentic SPHEREx observational data.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The pipeline automates several time-consuming stages of astronomical image analysis, making repeated observations easier to retrieve, align, and compare. It provides a practical approach for identifying potential transient or moving celestial sources, including asteroids and other objects that may require further investigation.

By reducing manual preprocessing and improving the consistency of image comparisons, our project can help researchers and astronomy enthusiasts explore large-scale infrared datasets more efficiently. It also provides a foundation for future candidate detection, validation, and classification systems.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of our project is combining real NASA SPHEREx observations, astronomical coordinate transformations, and multi-epoch difference imaging into one automated workflow. Rather than simply displaying astronomical images, our pipeline compares observations separated in time to reveal changes that may not be apparent in individual images.

Factors Considered

During development, we considered data reliability, observation dates, spectral-band consistency, missing pixel values, image dimensions, WCS coordinate accuracy, and alignment between epochs. We also considered the need to distinguish genuine changes from instrumental artifacts, noise, and alignment errors. Our results are treated as potential candidates rather than confirmed discoveries, allowing further scientific validation.
